metaData.originalTitle: 红筹退潮：中国互联网与全球资本的二十五年
metaData.title: Red-Chip Ebb: 25 Years of Chinese Internet and Global Capital
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article uses the VIE red-chip structure as its core thread to systematically review the 25-year history of capital migration by Chinese internet companies, from the birth of the Sina model in 2000 to the ebbing of red chips in 2026, analyzing the institutional, market, and geopolitical logic behind its rise and fall.
metaData.summary: Themed around the 'red-chip ebb,' the article deeply reviews the history of Chinese internet companies listing overseas via the VIE structure. From Sina's pioneering VIE model in 2000 to bypass foreign investment restrictions, to the awkward situation in 2026 where JOYY's market value was less than its cash reserves, the article presents a complete picture of this quarter-century-long capital migration. The author details the birth background of the VIE structure (immature Chinese capital markets, foreign investment access restrictions), its operating mechanism (contractual control rather than equity control), and how it provided a channel for US dollar capital to enter China's internet industry, spawning giants like Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, Meituan, and ByteDance. The article further analyzes the fragility of the VIE structure (the Alipay incident exposing that contracts could be unilaterally voided), changes in the Sino-US regulatory environment (Luckin Coffee fraud, the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act, China's new overseas listing filing rules), and the current trend of the red-chip structure receding—with many companies choosing to return to Hong Kong for listing or dismantle their VIE. Finally, it explores the practical considerations of dismantling versus not dismantling, and points out that the greatest legacy of the VIE is proving that the cooperation model of 'global capital + Chinese market' once existed.

mainPoints.point: The VIE structure was an institutional innovation for Chinese internet companies to list overseas, born in the dual crevice of regulation and capital.
mainPoints.explanation: In 2000, Sina pioneered the VIE model, using contractual control rather than equity control to bypass China's restrictions on foreign investment in the internet industry, paving the way for hundreds of subsequent Chinese companies to list in the US.

mainPoints.point: US dollar capital, via the VIE structure, provided non-consensus pricing power and sustained ammunition for China's internet industry.
mainPoints.explanation: US dollar capital could price business models (like Alibaba, ByteDance) that local capital could not understand at the time, and provided continuous financial support, fostering a burn-money-for-scale competition model that helped Chinese companies defeat US rivals like eBay and Uber.

mainPoints.point: The fragility of the VIE structure was exposed in the Alipay incident, showing that contractual control could be unilaterally voided.
mainPoints.explanation: In 2011, Jack Ma spun off Alipay from the VIE structure, proving that contractual control lacked absolute legal guarantees, shaking the foundation of trust overseas investors had in the VIE.

mainPoints.point: Changes in the Sino-US regulatory environment jointly ended the golden age of the VIE.
mainPoints.explanation: The US strengthened audit reviews through the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act, while China introduced new overseas listing filing rules, bringing the VIE under formal regulation, turning it from a 'shortcut' into a 'long detour' with significantly extended filing periods.

mainPoints.point: Currently, with the red-chip ebb, companies face the real choice of dismantling or not, but the VIE model is unlikely to reappear.
mainPoints.explanation: A large number of Chinese ADRs are returning to Hong Kong for listing or dismantling their VIE structures. New companies prefer to list directly using their onshore entities. Dismantling a VIE involves shareholder interest negotiations, tax costs, and control adjustments, with different companies making different choices based on their own circumstances.

keyQuotes: Apart from Chinese ADRs, there has never been a phenomenon in human history where a large number of companies from one country go to the securities market of another country to raise funds. It's like a great animal migration.
Gray means uncertainty, but gray also gives people the opportunity to solve problems creatively.
It is impossible to prevent the fusion of creativity, and it is impossible to prevent the flow of capital.
The market always prices before policy, but policy is never responsible for the market's advance pricing.

relatedArticles.title: A Comprehensive Guide to Microsoft Build 2026: The 'Agent-First' Era Arrives with Seven In-House Models
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Microsoft Build 2026 unveiled seven in-house MAI models, the Scout agent, the MXC system-level security sandbox, and Project Solara, marking the full implementation of an 'Agent-First' strategy.

relatedArticles.title: Dialogue with Minglue's Wu Minghui: AI is Killing SaaS, But I Found a New Path
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Wu Minghui, founder of Minglue Technology, believes that AI Agents will replace traditional SaaS, with the value of software itself approaching zero. The future business model will be open-source software combined with AI models and services, and he shares the practice and insights of his multi-Agent collaborative office platform 'Octopus'.

relatedArticles.title: In Conversation with DJI's Frank Wang: Seeking Truth, Finding Freedom, and Living a Story
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: In his first in-depth interview after a decade of silence, DJI founder Frank Wang reflects on his journey from a brash 'genius geek' to a mature leader, exploring core philosophies on management, organizational entropy reduction, and technological innovation.

relatedArticles.title: #461. A16z Founder Marc Andreessen: The World is More Malleable Than You Think, Deconstructing the "Hardcore" Management Philosophy of a Legendary Founder
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Silicon Valley's legendary venture capitalist Marc Andreessen deeply dissects the founder's spirit, founder-driven management models, and a16z's organizational innovation logic.

relatedArticles.title: A Conversation with Lee Kai-Fu: Don't Call Us 'Six Little Tigers,' Call Us 'Leopards'
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: In an in-depth interview, 01.AI founder Lee Kai-Fu reveals that after abandoning pre-training large models, the company pivoted to To B enterprise AI transformation services, achieving 250 million RMB in revenue in 2025 and over 1.5 billion RMB in orders for 2026. The company is preparing for an IPO and hopes to be called 'Leopards' rather than 'Six Little Tigers.'

relatedArticles.title: Ecosystem Differences in AI Entrepreneurship Between China and the US — A Conversation with Google Cloud's Head of Startup Ecosystem for North Asia
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Warren Li, Head of Startup Ecosystem for North Asia at Google Cloud, provides an in-depth analysis of the differences between the Chinese and US AI startup ecosystems, highlighting China's strengths in application scenarios and the US's leading position in foundational innovation and a high-tolerance environment.

relatedArticles.title: A Conversation with Dreametech's Yu Hao: My Real World
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article is a deep-dive interview by LatePost with Dreametech founder Yu Hao, systematically presenting the controversial entrepreneur's unique thoughts and practices on boundaryless expansion, the N+1 innovation methodology, brand premiumization, and constructing a new knowledge system to cope with an uncertain world.

relatedArticles.title: "The Biggest IPO in Human History": Is SpaceX More Than Just Rockets?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on SpaceX's prospectus, this article analyzes its $45 billion computing contract with Anthropic, its holdings of 18,712 Bitcoin, its board composition and aggressive governance structure, and the critical significance of the V3 Starship test flight for its valuation.

relatedArticles.title: AI Quarterly Report 26Q1: OpenClaw, the OpenAI vs. Anthropic Showdown, and Self-Evolution | LatePost Podcast
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Through an interview with Silicon Valley VC partner Henry Yin, this article provides an in-depth review of key AI trends in Q1 2026, focusing on the Agent paradigm shift triggered by OpenClaw, the product competition between OpenAI and Anthropic, and the profound evolution of AI self-evolution and the SaaS industry.
